extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining patent subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 using the MPEP two-step framework (statutory category then judicial exceptions), with factors and examples for products and processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step eligibility test
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two criteria for subject matter eligibility and both must be satisfied: (1) the claimed invention must be directed to one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter); and (2) the claim must not be wholly directed to subject matter encompassing a judicially recognized exception (laws of nature, physical phenomena, abstract ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the two-step analysis (Step 1: statutory category; Step 2: judicial exception/practical application). If a claim fails Step 1 it is not eligible, but if the disclosure suggests amendment to reach a statutory category, still conduct Step 2. Evaluate the claim as a whole under the broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four categories of statutory subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The four patent-eligible categories are: (i) Process — an act or series of acts or steps; (ii) Machine — a concrete thing consisting of parts or devices; (iii) Manufacture — an article produced from raw or prepared materials by giving them new forms/qualities/properties; (iv) Composition of matter — compositions of two or more substances or composite articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply court definitions (e.g., Gottschalk v. Benson; Burr v. Duryee; Chakrabarty) to determine whether the claim is directed to one of these categories. If clearly not within any of the four categories, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101, but still consider whether amendment could place the claim within a statutory category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-statutory examples (claims not directed to a statutory category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-limiting examples of claims not directed to one of the statutory categories include: transitory forms of signal transmission (e.g., propagating electrical/electromagnetic signal per se), naturally occurring organisms, a human per se, legal contractual agreements, games defined as sets of rules, computer programs per se, companies, and mere arrangements of printed matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite relevant precedent (In re Nuijten; Chakrabarty; AIA sec.33; In re Ferguson; Gottschalk v. Benson; In re Miller). Use these examples to identify claims that are not statutory; consider whether claim language or breadth would encompass such non-statutory embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims covering both statutory and non-statutory embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim whose broadest reasonable interpretation (in light of the specification and PHOSITA) encompasses both statutory and non-statutory embodiments embraces non-eligible subject matter and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a 'machine readable medium' claim that can be a compact disc (statutory) or a carrier wave (transitory, non-statutory) should be rejected when the claim as a whole encompasses non-statutory forms. Consider amendments to remove non-statutory breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions to the four categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicially recognized exceptions to §101 include laws of nature, physical phenomena, and abstract ideas; these are not patentable per se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Diamond v. Chakrabarty, Le Roy v. Tatham, Funk Bros., Benson, Flook, Diehr. Determine if the claim wholly embraces one of these exceptions; if so, it is not eligible unless limited to a particular practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical application requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that recites judicially excepted subject matter may still be eligible if it is limited to a particular practical application of that exception (i.e., how the exception is applied in a real-world product or process), rather than claiming the exception itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the claim as a whole to see if it recites a tangible/practical application and does not preempt substantially all uses of the exception. Practical application is demonstrated by limitations showing real-world use or structure (see Ultramercial, Diehr).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical application for products (machines, manufactures, compositions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Product claims (machines, manufactures, compositions) that are non-naturally occurring tangible embodiments and embody a particular practical application are typically evidence of eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tangible structural limitations in product claims often make practical application self-evident. Examples: a cup as a tangible application of containing liquid; a magnetic door latch as an application of magnetism. Conversely, product claims that lack tangible limitations and thus encompass the underlying concept are impermissible. After establishing a practical application, evaluate preemption and other patentability issues (102/103/112).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical application for processes (methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: A process claim must be limited to a particular practical application to be statutory under §101; merely reciting steps that occur in the real world does not guarantee eligibility if the claim effectively claims an abstract idea or preempts all practical uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bilski clarified that not every method is statutory; use the machine-or-transformation test and related inquiries as investigative tools. Field-of-use or token post-solution steps do not render an abstract method patentable (Flook, Bilski).

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test as an investigative tool
rubrics_metrics.description: The machine-or-transformation test remains a useful and important clue for determining whether some claimed processes are statutory: (1) tied to a particular machine/apparatus, or (2) transforms a particular article into a different state or thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test is not the sole test; consider additional factors from Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent. A claim satisfying the test weighs toward eligibility but failing it does not automatically mean ineligibility; consider totality of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors — machine/apparatus involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: When a method recites a machine or apparatus, consider: the particularity vs generality of the claimed machine elements; whether the machine implements the steps (integral use) vs merely being an object on which the method operates; and whether the machine's involvement imposes meaningful limits or is only extrasolution/field-of-use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For computer-implemented processes, a programmed general-purpose computer can be sufficiently particular if the claim conveys programming that creates a special-purpose computer (Alappat). However, merely adding a 'computer-aided' limitation without specifying how the computer aids or its significance is insufficient (DealerTrack). Extrasolution activity (e.g., mere data-gathering) typically weighs against eligibility (Cybersource, In re Grams, In re Meyer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors — transformation of a particular article
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether performance of the method results in or involves transformation of a particular article (physical object/substance or electronic data representing a physical object) to a different state or thing; such transformation weighs toward eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate particularity/generality of the transformed article, degree/type of change (different function/use vs mere relocation), the nature of the article (object/substance vs contractual/mental concept), and whether the transformation is merely extrasolution or imposes meaningful limits. Data manipulation that merely changes abstract values does not qualify, but changing data such that it has a different function or use can qualify (Bilski, Cybersource, Warmerdam).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors — application of a law of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Even absent a particular machine or transformation, a claim that applies a law of nature in a practical way may represent patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to Diehr and Bilski: determine if the claim embodies a practical application of the law of nature rather than claiming the law itself. Consider whether limitations tie the application to real-world use and avoid preempting the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-of-use and insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Field-of-use limitations (e.g., 'for use with a machine') and insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., generic data gathering) do not impose meaningful limits on claim scope and generally do not render an otherwise abstract claim statutory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A field-of-use is merely descriptive of environment and not a meaningful boundary (Bilski; Parker v. Flook). Insignificant activities that are not central to the inventive purpose should be discounted when assessing practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of preemption
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a practical application is established, assess whether the claim nonetheless impermissibly preempts substantially all practical applications of the judicial exception; claims that do so are not patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited occurrence of preemption must be evaluated. If a claim only covers a particular practical application and does not preempt substantially all uses, it is more likely eligible; if it covers substantially all applications, reject under §101. Use case law and claim scope analysis to assess preemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA Sec. 33(a) — prohibition on human organisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to the Leahy-Smith America Invents Act (AIA) sec. 33(a): 'Notwithstanding any other provision of law, no patent may issue on a claim directed to or encompassing a human organism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claimed invention as a whole encompasses a human organism, make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 and AIA sec. 33(a), indicating the claim is directed to a human organism and is nonstatutory. Form paragraph 7.04.01 may be used. Also continue to examine other issues pertinent to patentability (102, 103, 112) as applicable.
